summary: The note chronicles a local grassroots movement that fused civil rights and environmental justice, beginning in September 2023 in opposition to a proposed toxic waste facility near the minority-inhabited East Side. It follows key leaders, rallies, national alliances, youth education efforts, and the April 2024 passage of an Environmental Justice Act. It closes on the ongoing work of accountability and oversight.
one_line: A local movement linking civil rights and environmental justice grew from a 2023 protest into a 2024 Environmental Justice Act and ongoing oversight.
key_facts: The local activism began in early September 2023 at Greenway Park, led by Maria Gonzalez, a 58-year-old former teacher, and James Waterson, a young environmental lawyer.
The initial protest opposed a toxic waste facility proposed near the primarily minority-inhabited East Side district.
On October 15, 2023, Michelle Kim, a second-generation immigrant, gave a speech at City Hall on the disproportionate impact of environmental hazards on low-income communities of color.
Carl Jackson, a 70-year-old Vietnam veteran and activist, helped form the movement's backbone with Michelle Kim, organizing workshops and voter registration drives.
In late November 2023 the movement held the large-scale rally called the "March for Our Lungs" against environmental racism.
Dr. Luisa Ochoa, a 34-year-old pediatrician, said children in low-income areas were three times more likely to suffer from asthma, partly due to proximity to industrial pollution.
On February 22, 2024, the "Environmental Equity Summit" was held in town, attended by representatives from the NAACP, Sierra Club, and international delegates.

Aisha Brown, a 16-year-old high school student, started an environmental club and led her team to win the "Green Innovators' Challenge" on March 5, 2024, with a project on sustainable practices in low-income housing.

On April 20, 2024, the City Council passed a comprehensive "Environmental Justice Act" mandating stricter regulations on industries near residential areas and funding cleanup and green spaces in underserved neighborhoods.
After the Act, grassroots organizations and local government agencies formed "Green Zones" for green infrastructure, eco-friendly public transportation, and renewable energy projects.
Community oversight committees were created to monitor progress and hold regular public forums between residents and officials.
